content:Speaker user says: Today I’m jumping into the rabbit hole by posing a simple yet vexing question: Why is Young Rising Sons considered an ‘indie pop‘ band?
I’m not going to debate their talent, or bash their fan-base, or repulse you by assessing the ‘authenticity’ of their music. I don’t think they’re sell outs, and I’m not interested in diminishing the merits of their hard-earned success. But I’m convinced the word ‘indie’–contrary to common usage–is no longer an effective term to describe a band or it’s music. Rather, it’s been diluted into an overused marketing buzz word. My criticism isn’t aimed at Young Rising Sons, per say; it’s commentary on a confused record industry in decline, desperately attempting to push units.
The genesis of Young Rising Sons is about as typical as you can get: future band-mates Julian Dimagiba (bass), Steve Patrick (drums), and Dylan Scott (guitar), were childhood friends growing up in Red Bank, New Jersey. The chums were spurred to approach lead singer Andry Tongren about forming a band after attending an acoustic set at a local bar. Their debut single “High” was a breakout internet sensation that was paired with a viral black and white youtube video. This early success allowed the band to secure a record deal with Universal-via-Geffen affiliate Interscope, which incidentally represents a host of other ‘pop’ bands of a similar aesthetic: The 1975, Imagine Dragons, One Republic.
Young Rising Sons’ melancholy and reflective tunes tend to erupt in climactic choruses reminiscent of Disney film ballads with fittingly trite lyrics like “We’ll rule the world forever / together / with hearts of gold / who needs treasure.” Another trope bands tend to exhibit is sonic cohesion–the sound of the creative process coming together. Not here. Young Rising Sons’ individual musical contributions are as distinguishable track to track as the members of Bruno Mars’ studio band. Their overly balanced instrumental blend is clearly arranged to embellish Tongren’s vocal performance, which would be well positioned to tally up votes on an American Idol contest but point out like a sore thumb at a dingy rock club.
Perhaps it’s the circumstance of a dwindling old guard industry run by mega-corporations trying to cope with a failing music economy and trying to capitalize on the current craze–whatever you can do to make a buck is fine by me. If ‘indie’ is in, dress your bands in Levi skinny-fit jeans, doc martins, and fitted leather jackets and call it whatever you want big man. You’re in charge.
Young Rising Sons do have a full-length in the works, but I wouldn’t expect a heavy departure from previous output. Sometime during their hectic touring schedule, lead guitarist Dylan Scott announced his departure from the band. Tate Modern is a modern and contemporary art museum located in London, United Kingdom. It opened on May 12, 2000 and is housed in the former Bankside Power Station. The museum holds a large collection of contemporary and modern art from around the world, including works by artists such as Pablo Picasso, Salvador Dali, and Andy Warhol. 

The Bankside Power Station building was designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott and constructed in two phases between 1947 and 1963. After it was decommissioned in 1981, it lay dormant until a competition was launched in 1994 to redesign it as a modern art museum. Architects Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron won the competition and led a team to develop the award-winning design.

Today, Tate Modern is one of the most visited art museums in the world and attracts millions of visitors each year. It is part of the larger network of Tate museums, which includes Tate Britain, Tate Liverpool, and Tate St Ives. context:Matthew Williamson's project keywords: Tate Modern, art museum, contemporary art, London tags: design, Tate Modern

Pierre de Meuron was born in 1950 in Basel, Switzerland as well, and also received his architecture degree from ETH Zurich in 1975. They formed the architectural firm, Herzog & de Meuron, in 1978, and together have designed numerous landmark buildings around the world.

For the Tate Modern project, Herzog & de Meuron's design transformed the former power station into a dynamic art museum. They kept much of the structure's original industrial character, including its massive concrete walls and towering chimney, while adding a new glass facade that wraps around the building's north, east, and west sides. The architects also created a new entrance on the south side of the building, which leads visitors down into the museum's lower levels.

One of the most notable features of their design for the Tate Modern is the Turbine Hall, a vast concrete space in the heart of the building that serves as a centerpiece for the museum. This is the space that Matthew Williamson has chosen to showcase his fashion collection.

content:Speaker assistant says: Yes, of course! Here are some steps to help clean and maintain a wood stove:

1. Allow the stove to cool down completely before cleaning.

2. Remove ashes from the stove with a scoop or ash pan. Be sure to dispose of the ashes properly, either by burying them outside or placing them in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid.

3. Use a stiff-bristled brush to sweep the interior of the stove, removing any soot, creosote, or other debris that has accumulated. You may also use a vacuum cleaner with a brush attachment to clean the stove.

4. Clean the stove door and glass with a damp cloth and mild detergent. Avoid using abrasive cleaners, which can scratch or damage the glass.

5. Check the firebricks and replace any that are cracked or damaged. Firebricks help protect the metal stove from high heat and ensure that the stove operates efficiently.

6. Inspect the stovepipe and chimney for any physical damage, corrosion, or blockages that could affect the performance of the stove. Hire a professional chimney sweep to clean and inspect the chimney at least annually.

7. Replace the gaskets around the stove door if they are worn or damaged. This can help prevent air leaks and ensure that the stove operates efficiently.

8. Keep the stove dry and protected from moisture, which can cause rust or damage to the stove.

By following these steps, you can help ensure that your wood stove operates safely and efficiently. context:This material guide provides instructions for maintaining a wood stove, covering cleaning, repairs, and safety checks. keywords: stove cleaning, ash disposal, firebricks tags: stove maintenance, wood stove, chimney cleaning

content:Speaker assistant says: Step 1: Determine your internet service provider (ISP)

The first step in setting up a wireless network at home is to determine your ISP. Contact them to make sure they provide wireless access and to learn about the available services and packages. Most Internet providers have an option in their services that comes with a router.

Step 2: Choose the right wireless router

A wireless router is the hardware that transmits and receives signals for your wireless network, and it is essential to have a good one if you want your home network to work well. When selecting a wireless router, consider the range, the number of devices that can connect to it, the security features, and the compatibility with your ISP. Also, check the reviews and ratings of the model you are considering.

Step 3: Choose a security protocol

To protect your wireless network, you must select a security protocol. There are several types of encryption protocols; the best ones are WPA3, WPA2, and WEP. To ensure maximum security, use WPA3, because it is the latest and most advanced protocol. If your router has an older encryption protocol such as WEP, consider upgrading to a newer model.

Step 4: Install the router and software

Connect the router to your modem and turn on the router. Follow the manufacturer's instructions to install any necessary software on your computer or mobile device. Then, log in to the router's management page using a wired connection and set up your wireless network name, password, and security protocol.

Step 5: Connect your devices

Connect your devices to your new wireless network. If your device doesn't automatically detect the network, go to the wireless settings in your device's settings and find your network name. Enter the password from step 4.

Step 6: Test your connection

Test your connection to make sure everything is working properly. If you experience a problem, try restarting the router or moving it to a different location, farther away from obstacles or sources of interference. If the issue persists, refer to the troubleshooting guide provided by your router's manufacturer.

Step 7: Secure your network

To ensure your network remains safe, change your passwords regularly and make them strong. Additionally, use a strong password for your router's management page, and turn off the router's remote management feature.

In conclusion, setting up a wireless network at home is a relatively easy process that can significantly enhance your daily life if done correctly. By following the steps outlined in this guide, you can create a secure, robust network that will support all of your devices and provide you with seamless connectivity. context:964 keywords: wireless network, internet service, router, security, setup, connection, device tags: router_placement, Wi-Fi, signal, internet_service, connectivity

content:Speaker assistant says: Of course! Protecting your wireless network is critical to keep your devices and personal data safe. Here are some additional security measures you can take:

1. Change the default SSID and password: The first thing you should do is change the default network name (SSID) and password of your router. Easy-to-guess default passwords can be exploited by hackers. 2. Enable network encryption: As I mentioned earlier, use secure encryption protocols such as WPA3 or WPA2, and avoid using WEP, which is not as secure. 3. Set up a strong password: Your wireless network password should be at least 16 characters long, combining letters, numbers, and special characters. 4. Enable MAC Address Filtering: Restrict access to your network by allowing only specific devices or MAC addresses to connect, and create a whitelist. You can find the MAC address of your devices in the settings menu. 5. Disable SSID broadcast: Disable SSID broadcast so that your network is not visible to unauthorized devices. 6. Update your firmware regularly: Keeping your router firmware updated is essential to ensure security vulnerabilities are patched up. 7. 1. Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE): This is a new authentication method that replaces pre-shared key (PSK) authentication used in WPA2. Public Wi-Fi Security: For individuals who frequent public Wi-Fi, WPA3 also includes an optional new feature known as Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (OWE). OWE encrypts traffic passing over open Wi-Fi networks using temporary session keys. Overall, WPA3 provides enhanced wireless security, making it a more secure protocol for remote workers. This is especially important as remote workers often need access to sensitive company data and may work in public places such as coffee shops where they are at risk of being hacked. context:Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) keywords: WPA3, Wireless Security, Authentication tags: Security, Authentication

content:Speaker assistant says: Sure, I'd be happy to provide more information on Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE). SAE is a new authentication method used in WPA3 that replaces pre-shared key (PSK) authentication used in WPA2. It employs a new Diffie-Hellman key exchange technique known as Dragonfly, which makes use of elliptic curve cryptography. Unlike previous key exchange techniques that relied on a pre-shared secret (PSK), SAE allows the user and the access point to authenticate each other based on their knowledge of a shared secret that neither of them knows beforehand. This shared secret is a combination of a password and a salt. Here's how SAE works in practice:

1. A user attempts to connect to a Wi-Fi network protected by SAE. 2. The Wi-Fi access point and user exchange structures containing cryptographic elements. 3. The access point and the user exchange their secrets with each other simultaneously. 4. The access point and the user compute a password-based key exchange (PBKE) using those cryptographic elements and the shared secret. 5. The access point and user then compare their PBKE's to ensure they match. 6. If successful, the access point grants network access to the user. So, the unique aspect of SAE is that it prevents an attacker from potential security risks associated with pre-shared keys. An attacker could run brute-force attacks on PSKs that are too short or too simple to decipher, but SAE uses a more complex and secure key exchange method, rendering such attacks ineffective. SAE is designed to protect Wi-Fi networks against offline dictionary attacks, password guessing, and other known authentication-based attacks. By using a different method of authentication and key generation, it provides enhanced wireless security and makes it more challenging for an attacker to compromise the network. content:Speaker assistant says: I’ve been playing guitar and writing songs for as long as I can remember. As a kid, I’d strum my dad’s old acoustic in my room, dreaming of the day when I’d be a famous musician. As I got older, my skills sharpened and my musical influences evolved, but one thing stayed the same: my stage fright.

For years, I’d played small shows at coffee shops and open mics, nerves coursing through my body as I clutched my guitar and tried to sing on key. Every time, I’d shake and sweat and stumble over my words, leaving the stage feeling defeated and embarrassed. But deep down, I knew that my dream of being a musician would never come true if I couldn’t get over my fear.

So when I was offered the opportunity to play at a local festival, I knew it was my chance to face my fears head-on. The festival was huge – thousands of people from all over the country were expected to attend. My music was a mix of folk and indie rock, inspired by artists like Bob Dylan, Fleet Foxes, and Simon and Garfunkel. I’d been practicing my set for weeks, visualizing myself on stage and trying to calm my nerves.

But nothing could have prepared me for what it was actually like to perform in front of such a massive crowd.

Standing behind the stage, I felt my stomach churn as I listened to the cheers and applause from the audience. My bandmates – who, thankfully, were seasoned performers – patted me on the back and tried to calm me down. “You got this,” they said. “Just pretend it’s like any other show.”

But it wasn’t like any other show. My heart pounded in my chest as we walked onto the stage, the bright lights making me feel like I was in a dream. I could barely see the faces of the audience through the glare, but I could feel their energy radiating toward me.

And then we started to play.

Something strange happened as soon as we struck the first chord. Suddenly, my nerves were gone. The music took over, and I forgot about everything else – the crowd, the stage, even my own identity. I was just a vessel for the music, letting it pour through me and into the world.

I don’t remember much of the actual performance. I remember strumming my guitar until my fingers ached, my voice raspy from singing for so long. I remember the way the crowd sang along to our choruses, their voices melding with mine in perfect harmony. I remember the way the bass drum pounded in my chest, a steady reminder that we were still alive – still playing music in front of this massive, beautiful crowd.

When the set was over, I stumbled off the stage in a daze. People were clapping and cheering and shouting my name, but all I could think about was the feeling of pure, unadulterated joy that had filled me up on stage. I’d never felt anything like it before.

After that show, everything changed for me. I wasn’t magically cured of my stage fright, but I was no longer afraid. I understood that the fear was just a part of the process, that pushing through it was the only way to get to the joy on the other side. I kept playing shows – bigger and bigger ones each time – and each time, I felt a little bit more confident than before.

Now, years later, I’m still playing music. I’ve made it my career, traveling the world and sharing my songs with thousands of people. But no matter how big the crowds get or how far I go, I always remember that first performance – that feeling of raw, unfiltered joy that comes from truly giving yourself over to the music.
